issues.subcategory: contradictory operationalization of moral incongruence
issues.description: The manuscript defines moral incongruence in two incompatible ways. In the introduction and hypotheses it is defined as the interaction of moral disapproval and behavioral frequency, but later in the Present Study section it is described as the interaction of moral disapproval with severity of consequences. This creates ambiguity about the focal predictor and undermines interpretability and preregistration precision.
issues.quote:
The present work seeks to clarify if moral incongruence (the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior) ...

To accomplish this goal, we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study ... Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent coding of frequency scales
issues.description: The manuscript reports incompatible codings for the same frequency measures. In the Methods text pornography frequency is said to range from 1 to 6 with users defined as scores >1, but the supplemental instrument shows a 0 to 5 scale with Never = 0 and Once or Twice = 1. This affects inclusion criteria, centering, and interaction estimation.
issues.quote:
participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). Like the above-described process for the ASSIST, only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items described below.

[Pornography Viewing Frequency table:] | Never (0) | Once or Twice (1) | Monthly (2) | Weekly (3) | Daily or Almost Daily (4) | More than Once Per Day (5)

issues.subcategory: contradictory statement about who receives measures
issues.description: The manuscript first states that only participants endorsing past-year use will complete further problematic-use measures, but later states that problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. These two plans are incompatible and matter because they determine sample composition, zero inflation, and comparability across analyses.
issues.quote:
Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.subcategory: mismatch in gambling frequency measurement
issues.description: The methods claim gambling frequency will be measured by averaging across gambling behaviors, but the instrument shown contains a single item asking about any gambling behavior. There are no multiple gambling frequency items to average. This is a basic inconsistency in variable construction.
issues.quote:
We will assess gambling frequency using a single item. ... To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

[Supplement:] Gambled or placed bets at all

issues.subcategory: incorrect description of Holm adjustment output
issues.description: The manuscript states that bivariate correlations will be reported using 'Holm-adjusted test statistics'. Holm adjustment applies to p-values, not test statistics themselves. This suggests confusion about multiple-testing procedures and raises concern about implementation/reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: invalid or at least unjustified averaging across incommensurate ASSIST item metrics
issues.description: The planned substance problem score averages five ASSIST items that are on two different response scales with different numerical meanings (0-5 frequency items and 0/3/6 recency-coded items). Averaging these raw values assumes commensurability and equal interval properties that are not justified, producing a composite with unclear interpretation and distorted weighting of some items.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions ... on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day) ... Participants will also respond to two questions ... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: modified ASSIST used outside validated scope
issues.description: The study heavily modifies the ASSIST/NIDA Quick Screen and applies it to gambling and pornography, while acknowledging these uses are not validated. Because the main conclusions depend on cross-domain comparability, using an unvalidated adapted instrument for key outcomes threatens construct validity and makes domain comparisons uninterpretable.
issues.quote: We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST, in addition to the measures listed above. These will be included to allow fully parallel analysis across behaviors and substances ... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography ...

issues.subcategory: operationalization mismatch between self-perceived addiction and disorder symptoms
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames outcomes as 'self-reported feelings of addiction,' but for gambling it uses the PGSI, which assesses problem gambling severity rather than self-perceived addiction, and for substances it uses a modified ASSIST composite emphasizing problems/urges/control. These are not equivalent constructs, so cross-domain conclusions about 'self-perceived addiction' are not supported by the actual measures.
issues.quote:
we seek to establish whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction to both behaviors (i.e., gambling) and substances ...

problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index ...

To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST.

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measure inadequacy
issues.description: Moral disapproval is central to the theory, yet it is measured with a single item for each domain. Single items are especially problematic for nuanced constructs such as moral evaluation, shame, taboo, legal disapproval, or health-based disapproval. This limits reliability and may differentially function across domains, compromising comparisons of interactions across behaviors.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions ... For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: frequency windows misaligned across predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Behavior frequency is measured over the past 12 months, whereas most ASSIST problem items use the past 3 months, and the BPS uses the past 6 months. Interactions between moral disapproval and 12-month frequency are then used to predict outcomes from different time windows. This temporal mismatch weakens construct alignment and may attenuate or distort associations across domains.
issues.quote:
participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months ...

In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge ...

In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?

issues.subcategory: heterogeneous nicotine construct collapsed into one item
issues.description: The study combines cigarettes, smoked tobacco, smokeless tobacco, and e-cigarettes/vapes into a single nicotine/tobacco frequency item and a single moral judgment item. These products differ markedly in prevalence, social acceptability, and moral meaning, so collapsing them obscures construct meaning and may generate uninterpretable associations.
issues.quote: we will make it explicitly clear that smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine.

issues.subcategory: oversample not properly integrated into representativeness claims
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the total N>4,000 sample as nationally representative, yet 1,500 participants are an oversample of recent sports-wagering individuals. Unless weighted or analyzed separately, the combined sample is not representative of the U.S. population. This affects prevalence, regression estimates, and cross-domain comparisons, especially for gambling-related outcomes.
issues.quote:
The present work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500).

This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: no weighting plan for representative inference
issues.description: The sample uses YouGov matching and includes an oversample, but the analysis plan does not specify whether survey weights will be provided, how they will be applied, or whether estimates will be weighted/unweighted. Without this information, representativeness claims and inferential validity are impossible to assess.
issues.quote:
Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms. ... we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports ...

Data will be provided by YouGov in SPSS format. Accordingly, SPSS will be used ...

issues.subcategory: underpowered rare-substance subgroup analyses
issues.description: The authors acknowledge likely low effective Ns for prescription drug misuse and illicit drug use, with achieved power as low as .301 and .472 for the target SESOI. Yet they still plan equivalence-style conclusions, shifting thresholds post hoc if underpowered. These subgroup analyses are not adequately powered for the stated inferences.
issues.quote:
Prescription Drug Misuse | 3.5% | 140 | .057 | .301
Illicit Substances | 6%-12% | 240-480 | .032-.016 | .472-.764

Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects for the above behaviors, we will adjust analyses accordingly.

issues.subcategory: contingent post hoc redefinition of equivalence region
issues.description: The plan explicitly allows changing the equivalence bounds depending on observed data or power limitations, including redefining the region using the lower bound of the pornography interaction CI. This is a strong researcher degree of freedom that can favor desired conclusions and undermines confirmatory status.
issues.quote:
In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence ... we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects ... we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate of moral incongruence in predicting self-reported addiction to pornography

issues.subcategory: equivalence bound choice poorly justified and potentially on wrong metric
issues.description: The SESOI for equivalence testing is set to δ=.27 in one sentence, then later equated to β=.11 as the smallest listed effect, and discussed as an 'equivalence region to δ=|.11|'. The manuscript alternates among delta, beta, Cohen's d, f2, and ΔR2, with inconsistent values. It is unclear what metric the equivalence test actually uses and whether the chosen bound is correctly specified.
issues.quote:
we will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression ... with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

Given this variability, we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .25 ...)

Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent effect size conversion values
issues.description: The text gives different Cohen's d values for the same cited effect and appears to interchange effect-size metrics without valid conversion details. For example, one earlier summary lists Cohen's d=.22 for a study, then later the same study's smallest effect is described as d=.25. Such inconsistencies undermine the validity of the power/equivalence rationale.
issues.quote:
Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen’s d = .24 ...; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .22 ...)

Given this variability, we elected to set our SESOI ... equal to ... (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020).

issues.subcategory: OLS planned for bounded ordinal/count-like outcomes without clear justification
issues.description: Outcomes include summed BPS scores, averaged PGSI items, and averaged ordinal ASSIST items, all bounded and non-normal with likely pileups at zero. The primary plan nonetheless uses OLS moderation, with only vague mention of supplemental analyses if assumptions are violated. This is a poor primary modeling choice for these distributions and may bias estimates and standard errors.
issues.quote:
Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression ... will be tested ... Although Ordinary Least Squares techniques ... in large sample sizes are often robust against some violations ... in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses ...

As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package

issues.subcategory: supplement shows scoring discrepancies for validated measures
issues.description: The supplemental tables present nonstandard response codings for the PGSI and BPS relative to the methods text. For PGSI, categories are coded 0,2,4,5 rather than the standard 0,1,2,3; for BPS, categories are coded 0,2,4 whereas the methods text says 0 to 2. These discrepancies make it impossible to know how these measures will actually be scored and whether validated scoring will be used.
issues.quote:
problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index ... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always).

[Supplement PGSI:] | Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

Participants will respond ... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often).

[Supplement BPS:] | Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)

issues.subcategory: gender coding inconsistent and conceptually unclear
issues.description: The methods say gender will come from panel data, but analyses via the Shiny app will code gender as binary '1 = male, 0 = not-male'. This both departs from the listed covariate plan and collapses heterogeneous identities, while the survey itself includes separate conditional alcohol items for men and women. The coding is inconsistent and may affect model specification.
issues.quote:
Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov ...

Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates

issues.subcategory: problematic contamination of pornography outcome by moral guilt item
issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen includes an item about continuing use despite guilt. Because guilt may directly reflect moral disapproval/incongruence, the pornography outcome partially contains the predictor construct. This can inflate associations between moral disapproval and pornography 'addiction' relative to other domains whose outcomes may not include a comparable moralized item, biasing the central uniqueness comparison.
issues.quote: Brief Pornography Screen ... 5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional associations
issues.description: Despite acknowledging cross-sectional design, the manuscript repeatedly uses causal terms such as 'predict,' 'influences,' and claims that moral incongruence 'creates false-positive diagnoses' or 'affects' perceptions. Cross-sectional regressions cannot establish these directional claims, especially given reciprocal or common-cause explanations.
issues.quote:
we seek to establish whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction ...

should we find that moral incongruence does not predict any self-reports ...

it would suggest that community and population-based research using self-reported symptoms of addiction might be systematically biased by participant morality.

issues.subcategory: unaddressed confounding in claims of uniqueness
issues.description: The main argument is that a moral disapproval × frequency interaction being present for pornography but not other domains would support uniqueness. However, domains differ in legality, stigma, harm, social desirability, treatment-seeking, and measurement quality. Without modeling these confounds, differences in interaction size cannot be attributed to unique moral incongruence mechanisms.
issues.quote: should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model

issues.subcategory: equating non-significant/ equivalent interactions with theoretical uniqueness
issues.description: The theoretical claim of uniqueness is overinterpreted from planned statistical patterns. Failure to detect comparable interactions in gambling/substances could reflect lower reliability, lower variance, range restriction, weaker matching of measures, or lower power rather than true theoretical uniqueness. The manuscript does not sufficiently distinguish these alternatives.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.subcategory: misapplication of diagnostic caveat to support self-report model
issues.description: The paper links its planned findings to validating the ICD-11 CSBD moral-distress caveat. But the study does not assess CSBD diagnosis, clinical impairment, or differential diagnosis; it measures self-reported problematic use in a community sample. Therefore, the design cannot validate or invalidate a diagnostic caveat in the way claimed.
issues.quote: should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

issues.subcategory: overclaim from U.S. sample to addictions broadly
issues.description: The authors aim to speak about 'addictions more broadly' and moral incongruence across addictions, but the sample is U.S.-based and the substances/behaviors are a selective subset. Moral norms and stigma are culturally contingent. The discussion notes some cultural limitation, but the framing still overgeneralizes from one national context and selected behaviors.
issues.quote: the purpose of the present work is to test whether the moral incongruence model of problematic pornography use may generalize to addictions more broadly

issues.subcategory: community sample cannot address clinical false positives
issues.description: The manuscript highlights concern about false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings, yet data come from a general population panel plus sports-bettor oversample. Conclusions about clinical misdiagnosis, treatment seeking, or diagnostic decision-making are not supported by this sample.
issues.quote: the real potential concern associated with this effect is whether it creates false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings.

issues.subcategory: missing handling plan for oversample in analyses
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify whether gambling analyses will combine the representative sample and sports-betting oversample, model sample source, or conduct stratified analyses. Because the oversample differs systematically from the general population, this omission hampers evaluation of bias and comparability.
issues.quote:
we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses

issues.subcategory: missing details on exclusion criteria and quality control
issues.description: The authors rely on YouGov's proprietary standards and state they do not anticipate removing invalid responses. They provide no concrete thresholds for speeding, straightlining, duplicate prevention, bot detection, or other quality criteria. This reduces transparency and reproducibility.
issues.quote: As this data will be obtained via YouGov Opinion Polling, certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles

issues.subcategory: unjustified assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The manuscript assumes 'no unplanned missingness' and gives no plan for item nonresponse, skipped sensitive questions, or panel-data missingness. Sensitive topics such as pornography and illicit drug use commonly have missing data; lack of a handling plan threatens validity and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: unspecified supplemental analyses under assumption violations
issues.description: The plan says supplemental analyses will be conducted 'as appropriate' if assumptions are violated, but does not specify the alternative models, thresholds for violation, or criteria for choosing among them. This leaves substantial post hoc flexibility in analytic decisions.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: multiple outcomes and domain-specific choices without multiplicity plan
issues.description: The study proposes eight moderation analyses, multiple outcomes for pornography and gambling (validated and modified ASSIST), exploratory redefinitions of equivalence regions, and bivariate correlations, but gives no overall multiple-testing control plan for the main confirmatory hypotheses. This increases false-positive and interpretive flexibility risk.
issues.quote:
In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses ... with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items
Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: number of outcomes inconsistent with analyses count
issues.description: The paper refers to 'eight proposed outcomes' and '8 moderation analyses', yet Table 1 lists multiple dependent variables for pornography and gambling, and the text elsewhere emphasizes both validated scales and modified ASSIST items. It is unclear whether there are 8, 10, or more outcomes/tests, which matters for preregistration clarity and multiplicity.
issues.quote:
assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes.

In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses ...

Table 1 ... Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items
Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: table corruption prevents interpretation of power analysis
issues.description: Table 2 appears malformed, with repeated footnote text duplicated across columns. This makes it unclear what exact values correspond to which columns and undermines evaluation of the power analysis. Registered reports require precise, unambiguous tables.
issues.quote: Table 2 ... | 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health ... | 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health ... | 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health ...

issues.subcategory: comparison across domains confounded by non-parallel outcomes
issues.description: The central test of uniqueness compares pornography, gambling, and substances, but outcomes are not parallel: pornography uses both BPS and adapted ASSIST; gambling uses PGSI and adapted ASSIST; substances use only adapted ASSIST. Differences in interaction effects may reflect instrument properties rather than domain differences.
issues.quote:
These will be included to allow fully parallel analysis across behaviors and substances ...

Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items
Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval item may conflate legal, health, and moral judgments differently by domain
issues.description: The same wording 'I believe that using ___ is morally wrong' is applied to alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, illicit drugs, prescription misuse, gambling, and pornography. For some domains, respondents may answer based on legality or health risk rather than morality, and these meanings likely differ strongly across substances. This threatens cross-domain comparability of the moderator.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong”

issues.subcategory: selection restriction likely distorts interaction estimates
issues.description: If analyses are conducted only among past-year users for each domain, the design conditions on the moderator-partner variable and excludes nonusers who may have strong moral disapproval. This restriction of range can materially alter the moral disapproval × frequency interaction and complicates interpretation of 'moral incongruence'. The plan is inconsistent about this restriction and does not justify it.
issues.quote:
Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months ... will complete the remaining items described below.

issues.subcategory: goal-driven framing biases confirmatory interpretation
issues.description: The introduction states a 'specific goal of demonstrating' uniqueness of moral incongruence for sexual behavior. This framing is unusually directional for a registered report and suggests confirmation-oriented reasoning rather than an impartial test, especially given later flexible analytic contingencies.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.

issues.subcategory: no plan for scale reliability thresholds or remedial actions
issues.description: Although alpha and omega will be computed, the manuscript gives no thresholds for acceptable reliability or what will happen if reliability is poor, especially important for modified/unvalidated composites. This omission matters because reliability differences could drive apparent domain differences.
issues.quote: Descriptive statistics for included measures, as well as measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach’s alpha and Omega total), will be calculated
